title: Statement of the Problem: Format and Examples | AnswerThis
summary: The statement of the problem states your general problem, then lists specific questions. See the Philippine format, five steps and five examples.
body_markdown:
The statement of the problem is the part of a thesis that states the general problem your study addresses. It then lists the specific questions the study will answer.


This guide explains where the section goes and the format most Philippine schools use. It then shows how to write it in five steps and gives five examples you can follow.


## TL;DR


-


The statement of the problem gives one general statement, then numbered specific questions.


-


In most Philippine theses it is part of Chapter 1.


-


Each question must be answerable with the data you plan to collect.


-


Add hypotheses only for questions that test a relationship or a difference.


## What is the statement of the problem?


The statement of the problem tells the reader exactly what your study will find out. It has two parts. The first part is a general statement of the problem or the main aim. The second part is a list of specific questions that break the general problem into smaller pieces.


Every other chapter depends on this section. Your instrument collects data for each question. Your results chapter answers the questions in the same order. Your conclusions give one answer for each question.


The format in this guide is the one used in most Philippine schools. In many other countries, a “problem statement” is a single paragraph with no numbered questions. If you study in the Philippines, use the question format unless your manual says otherwise.


## Where does it go in a Philippine thesis?


The statement of the problem is part of Chapter 1. It usually comes after the background of the study and the framework. The hypotheses, the[significance of the study](https://answerthis.io/blog/significance-of-the-study) and the scope and delimitation usually follow it.


The exact order differs by school. Some schools place it after the conceptual framework and before the hypothesis statement. Check your own research manual before you start.


## What is the usual format?


Most schools ask for three parts, in this order.


1.


A general statement. This is one or two sentences that state the main problem or aim of the study. It should match your title.


2.


A lead-in line. This is a short line such as “Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following questions:”.


3.


Numbered specific questions. Each question covers one part of the general problem. A question can have sub-questions, numbered 1.1, 1.2 and so on.


In a quantitative study, the questions often follow a set order. Profile questions come first. Descriptive questions about each variable come next. Questions about differences or relationships come last.


## How do you write the statement of the problem in 5 steps?


1.


Start from the gap. Reread your background of the study. Find the one thing that is not yet known or not yet solved in your setting. That gap is your problem.


2.


State the general problem. Write one or two sentences that say what the study aims to find out, about whom, where and when. Use the same variables as your title.


3.


Break it into specific questions. Write one question for each variable or theme. Then add the questions that compare groups or test relationships. If you need ideas, see our[research question examples](https://answerthis.io/blog/research-question-examples) .


4.


Check each question against your data and analysis. For every question, name the data that will answer it and the method you will use, such as a mean, a t-test or a thematic analysis. If you cannot name both, change or remove the question.


5.


Add hypotheses where needed. A question that tests a relationship or a difference needs a hypothesis. Descriptive questions do not.


## Statement of the problem examples


The five examples below are invented for this guide. Each one uses a general statement, a lead-in line and numbered questions.


### 1. Quantitative example: study habits and Mathematics performance


*Title: Study Habits and Mathematics Performance of Grade 10 Students in a Public High School in Cebu City*


This study aims to determine the relationship between the study habits and the Mathematics performance of Grade 10 students in a public high school in Cebu City during School Year 2026 to 2027. Specifically, it seeks to answer the following questions:


1.


What is the profile of the respondents in terms of age, sex and daily study hours?


2.


What is the level of the respondents' study habits in terms of time management, note-taking and test preparation?


3.


What is the level of the respondents' performance in Mathematics?


4.


Is there a significant relationship between the respondents' study habits and their performance in Mathematics?


Question 4 tests a relationship, so it needs a hypothesis: there is no significant relationship between the respondents' study habits and their performance in Mathematics.


### 2. Quantitative example: hand hygiene among staff nurses


*Title: Knowledge and Practice of Hand Hygiene Among Staff Nurses in a Provincial Hospital in Iloilo*


This study aims to assess the knowledge and practice of hand hygiene among staff nurses in a provincial hospital in Iloilo. Specifically, it seeks to answer the following questions:


1.


What is the level of knowledge of the staff nurses on hand hygiene?


2.


What is the level of practice of the staff nurses on hand hygiene?


3.


Is there a significant difference in the level of practice when the nurses are grouped by ward assignment?


4.


Is there a significant relationship between the nurses' level of knowledge and their level of practice?


Questions 3 and 4 each need a hypothesis. Questions 1 and 2 are descriptive, so they do not.


### 3. Qualitative example: working students


*Title: Lived Experiences of Working Students in a State University in Davao City*


This study aims to describe the lived experiences of working students in a state university in Davao City. Specifically, it seeks to answer the following questions:


1.


How do the participants describe a typical day of work and study?


2.


What challenges do the participants face in balancing work and study?


3.


How do the participants cope with these challenges?


4.


What support do the participants need from the university?


A qualitative study explores experiences, so it has no hypotheses.


### 4. Qualitative example: sari-sari store owners after a typhoon


*Title: Recovery Experiences of Sari-Sari Store Owners After a Typhoon in a Coastal Barangay in Leyte*


This study aims to explore how sari-sari store owners in a coastal barangay in Leyte rebuilt their businesses after a typhoon. Specifically, it seeks to answer the following questions:


1.


What losses did the store owners experience after the typhoon?


2.


What steps did the store owners take to reopen their stores?


3.


What help did the store owners receive, and from whom?


4.


What lessons did the store owners learn about preparing for future typhoons?


The questions move in time order, from the loss to the recovery to the lessons. This makes the interviews and the results easy to organize.


### 5. Mixed methods example: an online reading platform


*Title: Use of an Online Reading Platform and the Reading Comprehension of Grade 8 Learners in a Public High School in Quezon City*


This study aims to determine the effect of an online reading platform on the reading comprehension of Grade 8 learners in a public high school in Quezon City, and to describe how the learners experienced the platform. Specifically, it seeks to answer the following questions:


1.


What is the reading comprehension level of the learners before and after using the platform?


2.


Is there a significant difference between the learners' pretest and posttest scores?


3.


How do the learners describe their experience of using the platform?


4.


How do the learners' experiences help explain the change in their scores?


Questions 1 and 2 are quantitative. Question 3 is qualitative. Question 4 joins the two sets of results, which is what makes the study mixed methods.


## How is it different from the research problem, objectives, research questions and hypotheses?


These five terms are close in meaning, so students often mix them up. The table shows what each one is.


Term


What it is


Research problem


The gap or issue that the study addresses.


Statement of the problem


The section that states the general problem and lists the specific questions.


Objectives


What the study aims to do, written as statements that start with “to”.


Research questions


The specific questions the study will answer. In this format, they are the numbered questions in the statement of the problem.


Hypotheses


Testable predictions for questions about relationships or differences.


Some schools ask for objectives instead of questions, and some ask for both. If your school asks for both, each objective should match one question.


## What are the most common mistakes?


-


Yes or no questions. “Do students use social media?” gives a one-word answer. Ask “How many hours a day do students spend on social media?” instead. Questions that start with “Is there a significant relationship” are the exception, because a statistical test answers them.


-


Questions the data cannot answer. If no item in your instrument collects the data, the question cannot stay.


-


Too many questions. A long list usually means the topic is too wide. Keep only the questions you need to cover the variables in your title.


-


Questions that do not match the title. Every variable in the title should appear in the questions, and no new variable should appear.


## Tools that can help you draft your questions


If you need a starting point, the AnswerThis[research question generator](https://answerthis.io/research-question-generator) suggests ten candidate research questions from your topic, your method and an optional population. You get 3 free runs. It does not search papers, so check each question against your own data plan.


For questions that test a relationship or a difference, the AnswerThis[hypothesis generator](https://answerthis.io/hypothesis-generator) drafts three pairs of null and alternative hypotheses, with 3 free runs. Treat them as candidates to edit, not as findings.


## FAQs


### What is the statement of the problem in research?


It is the section that states the general problem a study addresses and lists the specific questions the study will answer. In a Philippine thesis it is part of Chapter 1.


### How many questions should the statement of the problem have?


There is no fixed number. Use as many as you need to cover the variables in your title, and no more. Follow your school's manual if it sets a limit.


### Should I write questions or statements?


Most Philippine schools ask for questions. Some ask for objectives written as statements. Use the form your manual and adviser require.


### Is the statement of the problem the same as the research questions?


Not exactly. The statement of the problem is the whole section. The research questions are the numbered questions inside it.


### Where do the hypotheses go?


In many formats they come right after the statement of the problem. Our guide on[how to write a hypothesis](https://answerthis.io/blog/how-to-write-a-hypothesis) shows how to word them.
